summary: Precision agriculture - vision-guided spraying, yield prediction, autonomous equipment - is deployed at commercial scale. Who tracks it: federal adoption data, a UN benchmarking framework, a venture index, and standards bodies, layered over the equipment giants and AI pure-plays actually shipping it.

analysis.body:
The federal government's fortnightly AI-use survey does not currently publish a usable adoption figure for agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting: the Census Bureau's BTOS series marks the sector's share as suppressed in both the latest period and the prior one. The longer-running measurement layer sits at USDA's Economic Research Service, which publishes data series on precision-agriculture adoption across US farms, covering variable-rate technology, yield monitoring, and autonomous equipment. Globally, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization benchmarks digital agriculture through its e-Agriculture community of practice, focused on information and communication technologies for sustainable agriculture and rural development.

What gets deployed in the field is concrete and narrow. Carbon Robotics sells the LaserWeeder, which kills weeds with computer vision and lasers instead of herbicide, and describes its Carbon AI as powered by a Large Plant Model trained on data collected by LaserWeeders around the world. John Deere's precision agriculture line, including See and Spray and autonomous tractors, is the reference commercial deployment. Raven, a Brand of CNH, provides automated and autonomous farm technologies with AI path-planning and precision application. Climate FieldView, the digital farming platform, turns soil, weather, and yield data into planting and input prescriptions with machine learning, while Planet's daily satellite imagery and analytics feed yield prediction and crop-stress detection. AgGateway's standards work exists so AI models can ingest feeds from tractors, drones, soil sensors, and satellites through common identifiers.

Investment has stabilized but remains selective. Per AgFunder, global agrifoodtech funding hit $16.2 billion in 2025, almost flat versus the prior year at -3%, with investors directing capital toward companies with tangible science, real unit economics, and clear paths to revenue. The prior year reached $16 billion, a 4% drop from 2023. The geography is shifting: developing markets agrifoodtech funding grew 63% between 2023 and 2024 versus a 4% decline globally, and Asia-Pacific startups raised $4.2 billion as of the end of October 2024, a 38% increase on the $3.1 billion raised over the same period in 2023. Africa remains marginal, raising $145 million in the first half of 2024, a 1.6% year-over-year increase and just 1.6% of global investment, after a 62% decline in 2023 to $275 million. Deal count stayed nearly flat at 129 in 2023 versus 133 in 2022, indicating smaller deal sizes.

The ROI evidence in these sources is vendor-reported and specific. Climate FieldView states that farmers using its seed scripts saw an average increase of +5 bu/ac compared to users who wrote their own scripts. Carbon Robotics claims its systems reduce costs, eliminate weeds, increase yields, and improve farm sustainability, and notes its LaserWeeder retains all stock tractor controls with a manual-to-autonomous switch. Raven frames its precision agriculture solutions around productivity, sustainability, and profitability. None of these figures is independently verified in the material here.

The sources are largely silent on AI-specific risk and regulation. What exists is indirect: AgGateway describes its traceability and identifier work as contributing to food safety and regulatory compliance, and the Association of Equipment Manufacturers brings agricultural OEMs together to shape policy and develop strategies to combat environmental, political, and economic changes facing agriculture. A reader deciding whether to deploy should take from this that the sector has shipping commercial product, a federal and UN measurement apparatus, and investment that has stopped contracting but now rewards demonstrated economics, while the absence of a published Census adoption figure for agriculture means there is no current federal benchmark to lean on for how widely AI is actually in use.

https://www.aem.org/.brief: The Association of Equipment Manufacturers (AEM) presents itself as an organization advancing construction and agriculture equipment manufacturers in the global marketplace, with work in advocacy, safety, trade shows and events, and market data. It says it brings agricultural OEMs together to shape policy, understand data, and develop strategies for environmental, political, and economic changes facing agriculture. AEM also states it owns and organizes events that connect members with customers worldwide, and it has formed a cooperative effort with Messe Munich International to organize a leading international construction machinery exhibition in India. The page notes a 2027 AEM Product Safety & Stewardship Conference is scheduled to feature insights for product safety professionals. It describes four key service areas: advocacy, grassroots campaigns, public affairs, and research, connecting member companies with policy makers.

https://www.ispag.org/.brief: The International Society of Precision Agriculture is a scientific organization that develops technologies to help feed the world and improve quality of life. It offers a definition of precision agriculture in more than fifteen languages and gives members access to directories, networking, and discounted conference registration. Members receive a monthly “ISPA newsletter” that shares news, job listings, and event information, and the society is preparing for the 17th ICPA and 11th ConBAP in summer 2026. Country Representatives promote ISPA worldwide; applicants must email info@ispag.org with a bio, CV, and be current members, and members can post job announcements on the site and in newsletters.

https://www.planet.com/.brief: Planet Labs offers a platform called Planet Insights that brings together daily satellite imagery, derived data products, and cloud-based tools in one place. The company claims its imagery is the highest-frequency commercial Earth observation data, enabling daily monitoring, high-resolution tasking, and deeper derived insights. It says the platform lets users view the planet in time, space, and frequency, helping them make decisions quickly and confidently. Planet reports that organizations across many sectors use the platform to address operational challenges with a global, dynamic perspective.

https://www.ers.usda.gov/.brief: The USDA Economic Research Service site describes several data offerings. Its State Fact Sheets cover population, income, poverty, food security, education, employment, farm characteristics, financial indicators, top commodities, and agricultural exports for all states, with metro and nonmetro breakdowns and some county-level links. The Food Price Outlook provides food price data and forecasts changes in the Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index for food. A Vegetables and Pulses Data collection offers statistics on fresh and processed vegetables and dry pulses in the United States, along with some global data. The page also invites users to subscribe to email notifications for reports and news.

https://agfunder.com/research/.brief: AgFunder reports that global agrifoodtech funding reached $16.2 billion in 2025, down 3% year-over-year, with investors becoming more selective and favoring companies demonstrating "tangible science, real unit economics, and clear paths to revenue." While overall funding remained relatively flat, regional patterns diverged significantly: developing markets agrifoodtech grew 63% between 2023 and 2024, Asia-Pacific startups raised $4.2 billion as of October 2024 (a 38% increase), and African agrifoodtech showed mild recovery with $145 million raised in the first half of 2024 after a 62% decline in 2023. These trends suggest a sector undergoing consolidation, with capital concentrating in regions and companies meeting stricter investment criteria.

https://www.fao.org/digital-agriculture/.brief: FAO reports that the first stage of the Global AgriInno Challenge 2026 selected 13 youth-led innovation solutions from 137 valid applications out of 191 total, giving them a chance to pitch in China. The page explains that e-Agriculture is a global community of practice created from Action Line C7 ICT Applications of the World Summit on the Information Society, with FAO as its facilitator, and that its mission is to promote dialogue on the use of ICTs for sustainable agriculture and rural development. FAO also notes that three youth-led initiatives, AgriKonnekt from Kenya, Berikanpreneur from Indonesia, and a third unnamed, won the final pitch event in Hangzhou on 10 September 2026. Additionally, the page records that the 30th Session of the Committee on Agriculture (COAG 30) held in Rome from 20 to 24 July 2026 concluded after a week of high-level discussions on the future of agriculture and food systems.
